results.summary: This design is a basic logic tester that validates the operation of individual logic gates (AND, NAND, OR, NOR, NOT, XOR) and flip-flops (D, RS, JK). It provides common inputs for the gates and selection pins to choose which flip-flop to test, with outputs indicating the logic states. The design is intended for educational purposes, allowing users to verify truth tables by observing the outputs. It is implemented in Wokwi and requires no external hardware beyond the chip's pins.

This design animates a seven-segment display with a six-frame LED chaser pattern, using a configurable bank of clock dividers to slow the animation to human-visible speeds for any input clock frequency. It can also be used as a frequency counter. The chip requires an external clock source and a seven-segment display connected to its outputs, with optional DIP switches to select clock division factors. The design is notable for its wide range of supported clock frequencies and its robustness to noisy startup frames.

This design implements a 'Fastest Finger' game that determines which of eight buttons was pressed first. It uses a 3-bit counter and a 3-to-8 decoder to latch the first button press and illuminate the corresponding LED. The design requires external buttons connected to the inputs and LEDs (or a seven-segment display) connected to the outputs. It is a simple, clocked game suitable for educational or entertainment purposes.

This design is an 8-bit digital-to-analog converter (DAC) that receives data via a QSPI-like interface and outputs an analog voltage using an external R-2R network. It also breaks out bidirectional pins for external testing of delays and electrical characteristics. To use the DAC, the user must remove the on-board seven-segment display and connect an external R-2R network. The design is intended as an experiment and includes a simple serial protocol for setting the DAC value.

This design implements simple triple modular redundancy (TMR) voters with an error injection option. It includes one single D flip-flop, three TMR-protected D flip-flops, and one TMR flip-flop that allows error injection. The design is tested by setting inputs, triggering the clock, and observing outputs to verify correct voting behavior. It is a minimal experiment for studying TMR concepts and requires no external hardware.

This design takes 8-bit audio over a parallel port interface and generates an analog audio signal using PWM and a first-order sigma-delta modulator, similar to a Covox Speech Thing. It requires a 0.1uF capacitor to ground on the audio output pins for proper operation. The design has been tested in silicon and works as expected, providing a fixed-function sound card without the need for microcontroller firmware. It is notable for its simplicity and successful implementation in hardware.

This design implements free-running oscillators to compare simulation with reality and includes a true random number generator (TRNG). It uses combinational loops with dividers to produce output frequencies below 50kHz, and the TRNG output is available on one pin. The design is tested by selecting an oscillator via input pins and measuring the frequency on the output pins, while observing random numbers on another pin. It is a process experiment and requires no external hardware.

This design is a 4-bit pipelined Booth multiplier intended for learning purposes. It has been tested in silicon and verified to work correctly for all input pairs, with pipelining functioning as expected. The design achieved clock speeds of 146MHz at 1.8V and 154MHz at 1.9V core voltage. It is a simple educational project with no external hardware requirements.

This design is a multi-mode clock with a four-digit seven-segment display. It uses registers to divide the clock and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal for display, with the bottom 8 bits of the counter available on bidirectional outputs. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting the inputs to program a 24-bit compare register, allowing the counter to increment at different rates. It requires an external seven-segment display and a 10MHz clock source.

This design implements a single neuron in a binarized neural network (BNN), performing binary multiplication with XNOR, accumulation, and sign activation. It simulates the behavior of a neuron by accumulating XNOR results and applying a sign function to output +1 or -1. The design is tested by resetting the circuit and providing constant inputs and weights with an enable signal to begin the XNOR multiplication. It is a demonstration of BNN concepts and requires no external hardware.
